title: Treat questionable freshwater
overview: Clear water is not necessarily safe. Filtration and disinfection solve different problems.
materials: Pot and heat source, or correctly labeled water disinfectant
steps: Choose the least contaminated freshwater source available. Avoid water near chemical spills, floodwater, industrial discharge, or algal blooms.
Let muddy water settle, then carefully pour the clearer upper portion into a second container.
Pass water through clean cloth or a coffee filter to remove suspended particles. This does not remove germs reliably.
For clear water, bring to a rolling boil for 1 minute; above 6,500 feet elevation, boil for 3 minutes. Allow to cool naturally.
Store in a clean, covered container without touching the inside of the lid or opening.
warning: Boiling kills many disease-causing organisms but does not remove dissolved chemicals, heavy metals, or salt. A homemade sand/charcoal filter is not a validated purifier. If fuel is unavailable, use only a disinfectant specifically labeled for drinking-water treatment and follow its instructions.

title: Collect and store rainwater
overview: Collection is not the same as purification.
materials: Clean tarp or suitable roof catchment
steps: Place the catchment away from animal droppings, treated wood, and chemical runoff.
Slope the catchment toward a clean collection point.
Discard the initial dirty runoff, especially after a dry spell.
Cover collected water against insects and debris.
Treat rainwater as potentially contaminated before drinking, using an appropriate validated method.
warning: Do not assume rainwater from a roof is drinkable. Chemical contamination cannot be made safe by boiling.

title: Find east and west with a shadow stick
overview: Works with sunlight and a stable, roughly level surface.
steps: Plant the stick upright in level ground.
Mark the tip of its shadow with the first stone.
Wait 15–30 minutes, ensuring the stick does not move.
Mark the new shadow tip with the second stone.
Draw a line from the first mark to the second. It approximates west to east, respectively.
Face with the first mark to your left and second to your right; you are facing approximately north.
warning: This gives an approximate direction, not a precise bearing. Shadows can shift with season and latitude; do not rely on a single method for dangerous navigation.

title: Estimate time using the sun
overview: Solar noon is not necessarily 12:00 on a civil clock.
steps: Observe a vertical stick’s shadow over several hours.
Mark shadow-tip positions at regular intervals.
The shortest shadow near midday approximates local solar noon, assuming suitable conditions.
If you have a clock, label marks with clock times for that location and date.
Use the calibrated marks for rough time estimates on nearby days.
warning: Do not infer exact clock time from sun position without date, latitude, longitude, and time-zone corrections. The sun’s height changes by season.

title: Navigate by Polaris
overview: Northern Hemisphere nighttime direction-finding.
steps: Locate the Big Dipper if visible.
Find the two outer stars on the edge of its bowl (the pointer stars).
Follow their line roughly five times their separation toward Polaris.
Identify Polaris at the end of the Little Dipper’s handle.
Look toward the point on the horizon beneath Polaris for approximate true north.
warning: Polaris is not useful in the Southern Hemisphere and can be obscured. Confirm using other cues.

title: Build a basic A-frame tarp shelter
overview: A quick rain-shedding structure for mild to moderate conditions.
materials: Four or more stakes or secure tie-offs
steps: Choose elevated ground outside flood channels, away from dead branches and unstable trees.
Run a taut ridgeline between stable anchor points at a practical height.
Drape the tarp evenly over the ridgeline.
Stake or tie both lower edges outward to form a steep roof.
Tension corners and orient the narrow end toward prevailing wind.
Place insulation under sleepers; check runoff paths and ventilation.
warning: Avoid open flames and fuel-burning heaters inside tarp shelters. A tarp alone provides little insulation. Relocate rather than shelter under hazardous trees or in flood-prone areas.

title: Make a ground-insulated sleeping area
overview: Ground insulation often matters more than adding another blanket above you.
materials: Dry cardboard, foam pads, or dry vegetation
steps: Select dry, elevated ground.
Lay a moisture barrier beneath the sleeping area.
Add a thick, continuous insulating layer above the barrier.
Cover sharp edges and keep bedding off wet soil.
Keep the sleeping area ventilated and protected from rain.
warning: Do not use unknown chemically treated or contaminated scavenged materials against skin.

title: Evaluate a candle-and-metal heat diffuser
overview: A candle diffuser does not multiply heat; it only changes how heat is distributed.
steps: Estimate whether insulation and warmer clothing can meet the need without combustion.
If studying the concept, observe how metal becomes hot near a candle in a controlled, ventilated demonstration.
Compare temperature changes at a safe distance; do not touch hot metal.
Extinguish the candle before leaving the area.
warning: Do not use DIY candle heaters inside tents, small shelters, or while sleeping. Open flames, tipping, hot surfaces, oxygen depletion, and carbon monoxide are serious risks. Never seal a burning candle inside a container.

title: Warm a sleeping space without combustion
overview: Reduce heat loss before attempting to generate heat.
steps: Replace wet clothing with dry layers.
Insulate the ground beneath the sleeper.
Reduce drafts while preserving necessary ventilation.
Use a properly sealed warm—not scalding—water bottle wrapped in fabric if available.
Monitor for shivering, confusion, clumsiness, or worsening cold stress.
warning: Suspected hypothermia is an emergency. Do not apply direct high heat to numb skin or give oral fluids to someone unable to swallow safely.

title: Plan a small solar battery station
overview: A safe architecture begins with compatible ratings and protective devices.
materials: Solar panel with readable voltage/current label
steps: Write down the solar panel open-circuit voltage, operating voltage, and current from its label.
Identify the battery chemistry and nominal voltage; do not use damaged or unidentified cells.
Choose a charge controller explicitly compatible with both panel and battery chemistry.
Size cables and fuses to the device ratings and manufacturer guidance; install overcurrent protection near the battery positive terminal.
With all sources disconnected, verify polarity and wiring against the controller manual.
Connect in the manufacturer-required sequence; many controllers require battery first, then solar.
Measure output and confirm the controller reports normal charging before connecting a load.
warning: Never connect a solar panel directly to a lithium battery. Do not disassemble or rebuild salvaged lithium packs, bypass a battery-management system, or work on household mains wiring. Exact wiring depends on actual component models.

title: Bicycle generator: low-voltage concept
overview: Pedaling can generate useful low-voltage power, but output varies with speed and load.
steps: Secure the bicycle so it cannot tip or roll.
Identify a motor with known ratings and inspect for damage.
Design a guarded roller, belt, or chain drive so no clothing or fingers can enter moving parts.
Spin the motor by hand and measure open-circuit DC voltage with a multimeter.
Measure voltage at different speeds and determine polarity.
Choose a regulator and load matched to the measured voltage and current; test with a small protected load first.
warning: Do not attach phones or batteries directly to an unregulated generator. Moving chains, belts, and exposed wiring can cause injury. Never connect a homemade generator to building wiring.

title: Water and wind generator feasibility
overview: Measure the energy source before choosing a turbine or generator.
steps: For water, identify usable flow and vertical drop (head); never enter dangerous water to measure.
For wind, record wind conditions at the proposed installation height over time.
Estimate expected power using realistic efficiencies rather than peak claims.
Select an appropriately rated turbine and generator, with regulation and protective shutdown provisions.
Plan anchoring, guarding, flood protection, and safe maintenance access.
warning: DIY turbines can overspeed, shed blades, and create hazardous voltages. Water installations may need permits and can affect habitats. A heat-powered thermoelectric generator also requires a maintained temperature difference and suitable thermal protection.

title: Make an emergency listening plan
overview: Receive information before attempting two-way communication.
materials: Spare batteries or safe charging method
steps: Learn how to switch among AM, FM, and NOAA weather bands on your actual radio.
Scan for local broadcast stations while conditions are normal.
Write down reliable stations and the kind of information they provide.
Test reception at multiple positions, away from electrical noise.
Schedule brief listening windows to conserve battery.
warning: NOAA weather radio uses seven VHF frequencies from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz and requires a compatible receiver. A crystal AM radio cannot receive NOAA broadcasts.

title: Build a simple AM crystal receiver: planning guide
overview: A passive AM receiver is possible near sufficiently strong AM transmitters.
materials: Enamelled copper wire for tuned coil
Variable capacitor or suitable tuning circuit
steps: Identify the coil, capacitor, detector diode, and high-impedance earphone functions.
Choose a published, verified schematic matched to available parts.
Wind the coil to the schematic specifications and verify continuity.
Assemble the tuning circuit and detector on an insulated board.
Connect a safe antenna and listen while adjusting the tuning capacitor.
warning: Never connect an antenna to utility wiring or position it near power lines. Crystal radios depend on signal strength and are not reliable emergency receivers in all locations.

title: Start a small food garden
overview: Begin with soil, water, season, and realistic crop selection.
steps: Choose a site with sufficient sunlight and safe soil.
Check drainage and consider soil testing for contamination and nutrients.
Select crops suited to the local season and available growing time.
Prepare beds or containers and follow packet instructions for depth and spacing.
Water consistently, mulch where suitable, and inspect for pests.
Record planting dates, germination, and harvest outcomes.
warning: Avoid gardening in contaminated soil or using untreated human waste as fertilizer. Edible crops require safe irrigation water.

title: Identify wild plants cautiously
overview: A picture match is never proof that a plant is edible.
materials: Regional field guide with scientific names
steps: Photograph or sketch leaves, stem, flowers, fruit, and whole growth habit.
Record habitat, location, season, and whether multiple plants grow together.
Compare multiple identifying features against a region-specific botanical key.
Investigate toxic lookalikes and whether any required feature is missing.
If any uncertainty remains, do not consume or use medicinally.
warning: Never use taste tests to identify unknown plants or mushrooms. AI identification can be wrong. Avoid harvesting from roadsides, pesticide-treated areas, and contaminated water.

title: Plan humane live trapping
overview: Animal capture requires legal, welfare, and disease precautions.
materials: Contact for wildlife rehabilitator or animal control
steps: Identify the target species from multiple signs rather than tracks alone.
Check local trapping regulations and landowner permission.
Select an appropriate humane trap for the species and conditions.
Place the trap where non-target animals and children are unlikely to encounter it.
Check at intervals required by local law and animal welfare guidance.
Arrange safe, lawful handling or release with appropriate expert guidance.
warning: Improvised traps can injure animals and people. Avoid handling wildlife directly; bites, parasites, and zoonotic disease are risks. Rules differ by species and jurisdiction.

title: Preserve food without guessing
overview: Food safety depends on the exact method, acidity, temperature, and time.
steps: Identify the food and choose a tested preservation method.
For canning, use a current validated recipe from a recognized extension or food-safety authority.
Use pressure canning for low-acid foods when the tested recipe requires it.
Follow exact jar size, process time, pressure, and altitude adjustments.
Label and store properly; discard suspect food without tasting.
warning: Do not invent canning times or substitute water-bath canning for pressure canning. Botulism toxin may be present without visible spoilage.

title: Identify and test a salvaged DC motor
overview: Learn the difference between a motor, generator, and alternator.
steps: Disconnect equipment from all power sources; do not open sealed batteries or mains-powered capacitor sections.
Inspect the motor for damage, corrosion, and readable labels.
Record rated voltage, current, and model if present.
Measure winding continuity with a multimeter on an unpowered motor.
If it is a permanent-magnet DC motor, rotate the shaft by hand and measure small generated voltage.
warning: Appliances may retain dangerous charge after unplugging. Do not salvage parts from microwaves, CRT televisions, or high-voltage power supplies without qualified supervision.

title: Build a battery-free AM crystal radio
overview: Assemble a receive-only loop crystal set for learning how a tuner and detector recover AM audio.
materials: Medium-wave AM loop and matching variable capacitor from a crystal-radio kit
1N34A germanium detector diode or the kit-specified detector
High-impedance crystal earpiece with its kit-specified shunt resistor
Dry nonconductive base, short leads, and a multimeter
steps: Identify two nodes from the kit drawing: the tuned node and the return. Connect the loop and tuning capacitor in parallel between these nodes.

Connect the diode anode to the tuned node and its banded cathode to the audio node. Connect the earpiece between the audio node and return. Put the specified shunt resistor across the earpiece to give the detector a DC return.
Use the kit drawing to verify the joints and ensure there is no accidental short across the earpiece or the capacitor plates. The loop itself may show low DC resistance across the tuning nodes.

Rotate the loop indoors as you sweep the tuning capacitor. Compare against a known local AM station you can receive on a separate radio. If there is silence, check the earpiece type, loose connections, tuner movement and station strength first.
warning: Use a self-contained indoor loop. Keep it away from mains, electrical wiring and outdoor antennas. This experiment depends on local AM signal strength and cannot receive FM or NOAA weather alerts.

sources.title: New Jersey Antique Radio Club · Crystal Set Projects, loop receiver

title: Assemble and test a hand-crank receiver
overview: Pair a manufacturer-regulated hand-crank USB power source with a compatible small receiver. A suitable model can serve as a backup listening setup.
materials: Hand-crank USB generator or power bank with documented regulated output and protected storage
Receiver with a manufacturer-approved USB power input and documented current requirement
Manufacturer-approved cabled connection, USB meter, enclosure or strap, and backup batteries
steps: Confirm that the source and receiver agree on the required USB voltage and current. Check whether the receiver can listen while externally powered. Select a model explicitly supporting NOAA Weather Radio and standby alerting if that is your requirement.
Mount the two finished units in a ventilated carrier with the antenna, controls and crank unobstructed. Secure the cable so pulling on it does not strain either port.

Use the crank only as directed by its manual to charge the protected store. Measure the USB output under the receiver load if you have a suitable inline meter. Verify the receiver starts, stays tuned, and does not repeatedly reboot.

At a fixed volume, record the elapsed listening time after a timed crank session. Test voice reception and any alert feature separately. Keep a known-good battery supply available and repeat the test before relying on the kit.
warning: Use intact commercial power hardware. Never wire a bare generator to batteries or the receiver. Stop if the source overheats, the receiver resets, or the output falls outside its specified range.

title: Practice a walkie-talkie check-in
overview: Set up a U.S. family or group radio drill with certified handhelds, a check-in schedule and a fallback.
materials: Two compatible certified radios and their manuals
steps: Identify each radio service from its label or documentation. For a U.S. FRS exercise use certified FRS radios. GMRS generally requires an FCC license.
Agree on a primary channel, backup channel, check-in time and meeting place. For the first test disable the tone or code on both radios to make setup easier.
Listen before transmitting. Press push-to-talk, pause briefly, and speak: “Base, this is Team One. Radio check. Over.” Release the button and wait for readback.
Test at both intended locations. Record where the channel works and where it drops out. Rehearse moving to the backup channel at the scheduled time after a missed check-in.
For short reports, give location, time, what happened and what help you need. Ask the receiver to repeat critical details.
warning: U.S. guidance. Tone codes filter received audio and do not create privacy. Keep sensitive details off shared channels. For emergencies use 911 when reachable. Do not assume anyone monitors your channel.

title: Set up NOAA Weather Radio alerts
overview: Verify local forecast audio and standby alerts on a compatible receiver ahead of severe weather.
materials: Backup batteries and local transmitter information
steps: With the antenna extended as directed, scan the weather channels and listen for the strongest clear local broadcast. Record the frequency and station.
If the model supports SAME, enter the county or area codes from the official NWS listing and confirm which alerts the model has enabled.
Put the set in alert standby and confirm reception of a scheduled local test where available. Test the receiver again on backup batteries and in the room where you will use it.
warning: Weather-band reception and automatic alerting are separate features. Keep another way to receive alerts in case coverage, equipment or power fails.
